resources.string: Motor or brake current is within 30 % of the absolute maximum current, so current peaks can trip overcurrent faults.
The slow absolute current limit makes damage to the controller much more likely.
Overmodulation above 1.15 adds a lot of distortion for little gain.
Battery cutoff start is not above cutoff end, so current is never reduced as the battery empties.
Battery cutoff end is below %1$s V, the empty voltage of %2$d cells, so the cells can be discharged too far.
Battery cutoff start is above %1$s V, the full voltage of %2$d cells, so current is reduced even on a full battery.
%1$d cells are %2$s V when full, above Maximum Input Voltage. The controller stops with an overvoltage fault on a full battery or when braking.
Battery cutoff end is below Minimum Input Voltage, so the controller cuts out at once before the cutoff has reduced the current.
MOSFET temperature cutback start is not below its end, so current is cut at once instead of gradually.
Motor temperature cutback start is not below its end, so current is cut at once instead of gradually.
Maximum duty cycle is not above the minimum duty cycle, so the motor can\'t run.
The motor reaches about %1$s ERPM at maximum duty on a full battery, so this limit never acts.
A current limit is above what this hardware allows; the controller will lower it.
Maximum Input Voltage is above what this hardware allows, so a full battery can damage the controller.
An ERPM limit is above what this hardware allows; the controller will lower it.
Maximum duty cycle is above what this hardware allows.
